segments.say: Think about brushing your teeth. Do you procrastinate on it? Probably not. You don't sit in the bathroom thinking, I really should brush my teeth, but I'm just not in the mood. You simply do it, almost without thinking. It's a habit. And habits are one of the most powerful tools we have against procrastination.

The psychologist Wendy Wood has spent many years studying habits. In one diary study, published in two thousand and two with her colleagues, participants regularly recorded what they were doing and thinking throughout the day. And the researchers estimated that about forty three percent of daily behaviors were performed almost daily, in the same context, often while people were thinking about something else.

show.who: Wendy Wood, Jeffrey Quinn & Deborah Kashy
show.where: Published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2002
show.what: Participants recorded what they were doing, thinking and feeling at regular intervals through the day, in a diary study.

segments.say: In other words, a large part of what we do every day runs on autopilot. Habits are behaviors that have become linked to particular situations, through repetition. When the situation appears, the behavior follows, without much conscious thought, and without needing motivation or willpower.

show.cap: Same place, same time, same action

segments.say: And here's why that matters for procrastination. Procrastination happens at the moment of decision. Should I do this now? And habits remove that moment. When a task is a habit, there's no decision to make. So there's no opportunity for the urge to avoid to win. You just find yourself doing it.

How do habits form? Through repetition in a stable context. Doing the same thing, in the same place, at the same time, triggered by the same cue. Over time, the cue and the action become linked in memory. Research by Phillippa Lally and colleagues, published in two thousand and ten, suggested that forming a habit can take a while. On average around two months in their study, with large differences between people and behaviors.

That's worth knowing, because many people have heard that habits form in twenty one days. In Lally's study, the average was closer to sixty six days, and the range was wide, from a few weeks to many months. So if a new habit doesn't feel automatic after three weeks, that's normal. Keep going. It's getting stronger, even if you can't feel it yet.

Lally's study also found something reassuring. Missing a single day didn't seriously damage the habit forming process. You don't have to be perfect. What matters is getting back to the routine soon after a slip. Remember self forgiveness. A missed day is just a missed day, not a reason to quit.

One helpful way to build a new habit is to anchor it to something you already do every day. After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write for ten minutes. After I brush my teeth at night, I'll lay out tomorrow's clothes. The existing routine becomes the cue. It's a lot like the if then plans we discussed earlier.

Wood's research also emphasizes the power of the environment. Making the desired behavior easy, and the undesired one harder. If you want to read more, leave a book on your pillow. If you want to exercise in the morning, sleep near your running clothes. Small changes in the environment can shape habits more than willpower ever could.

There's something peaceful about this. Instead of fighting yourself every day, you build a few simple routines that carry you along. The hard work of deciding happens once, at the beginning. After that, the habit does the work. And you're free to put your energy into the parts of life that truly need your attention.

So here's what habit research teaches us. A large share of our daily actions are habitual. Habits remove the moment of decision, where procrastination usually wins. In one study, forming a habit took around sixty six days on average, with big differences. And anchoring new habits to existing routines, and making them easy, can help them stick.

segments.say: And even with good habits, some tasks are long and demanding. Is there a way to make long work feel less like a mountain? A simple method named after a kitchen timer, and some research on attention, offer a gentle answer.
